beats.script_body: At the top end of Fifth Avenue's Museum Mile, in East (Spanish) Harlem—El Barrio—this museum started life modestly in 1969 as a place to curate and display the art and history of New York's Puerto Rican community. Signage on the exhibits is in both English and Spanish.

beats.script_body: One of the world's largest cathedrals has a floor area of 121,000 square feet and a 232-foot-high vault. Built in fits and starts beginning in 1892, in a mixture of Gothic, Romanesque, and Byzantine styles, it is still only two-thirds complete. On Wednesdays and Fridays at noon and on Saturdays at noon and 2 p.m., you can climb 124 feet up spiral staircases to the top of the cathedral to study the architecture and stained-glass windows.

beats.poi_name: General Ulysses S Grant National Memorial
beats.script_body: A grand, granite mausoleum overlooking the Hudson River in the north of Riverside Park is the final resting place of President Ulysses S. Grant and his wife, Julia. The tomb—the largest in North America—was completed in 1897 and is engraved with the words "Let us have peace," a line from Grant's speech to the 1868 Republican Convention that became his campaign slogan. When the former Civil War general died in 1885, around 90,000 people donated more than $600,000 to build his tomb—then the largest public fundraising effort in U.S. history.

beats.script_body: New York's first African-American Baptist church offers the chance to listen to one of the nation's finest gospel choirs. Founded in 1808 by a group of African Americans and Ethiopian sea merchants, Harlem's most prominent church has more than 4,000 parishioners. If you wish to attend the 11 a.m. Sunday service, get there early; parishioners get first dibs on the church's 1,000-odd seats, and the visitors' line typically stretches around the block.

beats.script_body: Built in 1765, this Georgian-style mansion served as home and battle headquarters to George Washington in 1776. Located on a hilltop overlooking the Hudson River, it gave Washington a strategic advantage in the Battle of Harlem Heights against the British. Inside the house—Manhattan's oldest personal residence—each room is decorated to re-create a part of its history, including the colonial period, the Revolutionary War, and the new republic.

beats.script_body: The remains of five French cloisters and other religious sites were shipped from Europe in the early 20th century by an American collector and bought by the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 1925, then added to subsequently. The collection of medieval European art and architecture—around 3,000 pieces from the ninth to the 16th centuries—is arranged in chronological order. Set above the Hudson River in Upper Manhattan's Fort Tryon Park, the whole site is invitingly small, and its displays can be viewed in a single visit.

beats.script_body: Starting at the turn of the century, African Americans from across the country, especially the South, moved north to seek better lives, settling in Harlem beginning around 1910. Over time many made their voices heard as poets, intellectuals, and musicians in what became known as the Harlem Renaissance. One of the most successful authors of the period was Langston Hughes; with poems such as "The Negro Speaks of Rivers," he wrote about what it was like to be black in America and encouraged others to do the same. Zora Neale Hurston was the leading black female writer of the period, best known for Their Eyes Were Watching God, one of the first novels based on a black woman's voyage of self-discovery. In 1925, African-American professor Alain Locke edited a collection of poems and essays by black writers called The New Negro; the book shattered stereotypes and was key to defining the Harlem Renaissance. Locke wrote that in Harlem, "Negro life is seizing upon its first chances for group expression and self-determination."

beats.script_body: Southern blacks brought new rhythms north with them. Jazz musicians and singers including Louis Armstrong, Bessie Smith, and Duke Ellington performed at clubs and theaters, some of which—such as the Cotton Club and the Roseland Ballroom—only served white patrons. Black theater also had a renaissance: in 1921 Shuffle Along became the first all-African-American musical to play on Broadway, before a white audience, and led to more firsts for African Americans in the medium.
